idiom_name: Collection<T> subclass overriding InsertItem/SetItem/RemoveItem/ClearItems + IReadOnlyList<T> exposure
implementation_notes: System.Collections.ObjectModel.Collection<T> exists for exactly this job: derive from it, override the protected InsertItem/SetItem/RemoveItem/ClearItems hooks, and every public mutation path (Add, Insert, Remove, RemoveAt, Clear, indexer set) is funnelled through your validation - the base class keeps the interface plumbing (IList<T>, ICollection<T>, enumeration, indexer). Expose reads as IReadOnlyList<T>, and make the wrapper-versus-snapshot choice explicitly: ReadOnlyCollection<T> (or AsReadOnly()) is a live wrapper over the same store, so later changes through the owner remain visible, while ToArray() or a copied List<T> is a snapshot that isolates the caller at the cost of one allocation. Keep the inherited Items property private to the class - an IList<T> that reaches a caller is the leak the pattern exists to prevent.
pitfalls: Items (IList<T>) is reachable from subclasses and from any IList<T> upcast of the object: returning it lets callers add without validation; validate in the overrides and publish only IReadOnlyList<T>.
ReadOnlyCollection<T> is a live wrapper, not a copy: mutations through the owner stay visible to holders, and neither class is thread-safe.
Collection<T> accepts null and duplicates by default; reject both explicitly if the domain forbids them.
System.Text.Json and other serializers describe the mutable shape; project to a DTO if the wire contract must not expose Add/Remove.
